title: @Elyse | theatre & shakespeare  #shakespeare #theatre #romeoandjuliet
transcript: What if Romeo and Juliet were set at the border wall between Mexico and the US? That's the buzzy concept behind this Shakespeare in the park production, but not to great effect, in my opinion. I sometimes call productions like this the “Landlord Special” Shakespeare. Or as one of my mutuals, Elyse Sharp, calls it, bumper sticker Shakespeare. Where the concept is kind of indiscriminately slathered over the play or slapped on like a bumper sticker without really doing the work to consider the granular implications in the world of the play. Now, to be fair, this Romeo and Juliet was far from the most egregious example of the landlord special I've ever seen. There are ways in which the director, Saheem Ali, extended the concept beyond just the staging. I actually really liked how they strategically translated sections of it into Spanish, especially when Romeo was at his most poetic and expressive, And I like the dynamic of Juliet sometimes trying to speak her imperfect Spanish back to him. And on the most superficial level, sure, we understand that the issue of immigration is at the centre of the dispute between the Montagues and the Capulets, but I, at least, was a little confused about how, specifically, that was supposed to map on. The Montagues and the Capulets are, after all, on the same side of the border wall. And I guess on the U S. Side? although that wasn't super clear. I wasn't sure what modern equivalent they were trying to connect the Capulets to; who exactly they were within the world of this play and the nature of their proximity to power and their relationship to the Montagues was a little muddy and undercooked. And even the fact that they are, I guess, in a position of privilege or power compared to the Montagues kind of goes against the whole “two households both alike in dignity” thing. To be clear, as a staunch anti-purist, I'm happy to see a director try their hand at imposing a different power dynamic than the one Shakespeare intended. But it requires more thoughtful and hands on retooling than this production had. So even though it has this subversive concept, the production plays in practice like a fairly run-of-the-mill Romeo and Juliet. One thing I do think they did well was that a lot of productions kind of struggle to keep up the momentum after Tybalt's death. Cause the first half is kind of front-loaded with a lot of the best scenes, and it's famously more comedic and entertaining than the second half. So it can be really tough to navigate the tonal shift into the more serious second half Which also consists of a lot of two person scenes where someone is bemoaning how terrible their situation is. But I actually think this production managed a more smooth tone and pacing. Is that because the first half is a little less energetic and funny than most productions? Partly, yes, but they reap the benefits of it in the second half, where the events between Tybalt's death and Romeo's death feel like a more slow, continuous build.
reasoning: The reviewer critiques the central concept as underdeveloped 'bumper sticker Shakespeare' and calls the production 'run-of-the-mill,' but credits some directorial choices like the Spanish translations and the second-half pacing. Neither a clear recommendation nor a pan.
